reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Characterised by effortless, repetitive regurgitation of recently ingested food into the mouth, where it is re-chewed, re-swallowed, or spat out
Regurgitation typically begins within minutes of eating, is not preceded by nausea or retching, and involves undigested, pleasant-tasting food
Symptoms usually cease once the regurgitated material becomes acidic, distinguishing it from vomiting and gastro-oesophageal reflux
High-resolution manometry with impedance may capture the diagnostic postprandial rise in intragastric pressure (abdominal straining) coinciding with retrograde flow
It is a behaviourally learned, often unconscious contraction of the abdominal wall, not a structural or acid-driven disease
First-line treatment is diaphragmatic-breathing behavioural therapy, which competes with and suppresses the abdominal straining
Frequently misdiagnosed as refractory reflux or gastroparesis, leading to unnecessary acid suppression and procedures
reference.pathophysiology: Rumination syndrome results from a subconsciously acquired increase in intra-abdominal pressure, produced by contraction of the abdominal wall musculature after eating. This straining, combined with transient relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter, propels gastric contents retrograde into the oesophagus and mouth without the coordinated antiperistalsis and autonomic prodrome of true vomiting. Because the behaviour is a learned somatic response rather than a mucosal or motility disease, the regurgitated material is undigested and non-acidic, and the pattern can be interrupted by teaching competing diaphragmatic breathing.
additionalDifferentials: Gastroparesis and other gastric motility disorders
Achalasia or other oesophageal outflow obstruction
Eating disorders such as bulimia nervosa
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution oesophageal manometry with impedance, ideally postprandial, to demonstrate the characteristic pattern
Upper endoscopy to exclude mucosal disease and mechanical obstruction
Gastric emptying study to differentiate from gastroparesis
Ambulatory pH-impedance monitoring to distinguish from acid reflux
Nutritional and psychological assessment where weight loss or comorbidity is present
redFlags: Significant weight loss, dehydration, or nutritional compromise
Nocturnal or truly acidic regurgitation suggesting reflux or another organic cause
Dysphagia, odynophagia, or evidence of mechanical obstruction
Features suggesting a primary eating disorder requiring specialist care
reference.prognosis: The disorder is benign and highly responsive to behavioural therapy, with many patients achieving marked or complete symptom control; delayed recognition, however, exposes patients to needless investigations and treatments.
pitfalls: Labelling the regurgitation as refractory reflux and escalating acid suppression
Ordering repeated procedures instead of recognising the postprandial effortless pattern
Confusing the condition with an eating disorder or with true vomiting
Overlooking coexisting anxiety or psychological factors that reinforce the behaviour
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Rome Foundation diagnostic criteria for functional gastrointestinal disorders
management: Diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing behavioural therapy as first-line treatment to compete with and suppress the post-prandial abdominal straining
Patient education and reassurance that the disorder is a learned behaviour rather than a structural or acid-driven disease
Biofeedback, using postprandial manometry where available, to reinforce and consolidate the breathing technique
Habit-reversal therapy and management of any psychological comorbidity, with clinical psychology input
Baclofen as an adjunct in refractory cases to reduce transient lower oesophageal sphincter relaxations
Nutritional assessment and support where weight loss or nutritional compromise has occurred
